title: Evaluation Methodology
scopeHtml: Scope: Datasets, graders, LLM-as-judge, metrics, regression and online evaluation.

notes.title: Why evals come first
notes.html:
Definition. An eval is a fixed collection of test cases with expected behaviour and a grader that turns model outputs into scores. It makes quality measurable and comparable across prompts, models, retrieval settings and code changes.

Why LLM systems need them more than normal software. Outputs are non-deterministic and open-ended; "it looks fine on my five examples" hides failures; changes (prompt tweak, model update) have non-obvious side effects; stakeholders need evidence; and without an eval you cannot tell whether an optimization (cheaper model, shorter prompt) hurt quality.

Eval-driven development loop.

  1. Define success criteria (specific, gradable).
  2. Build the eval set and graders before the feature.
  3. Baseline simple solution → measure.
  4. Change one thing → measure → keep or revert.
  5. Gate releases on the eval; monitor in production; feed failures back.

Expectations. The first score is often poor (2 to 4 out of 10 is normal); what matters is a trend of improvement and understanding failure categories.

Real life. A thermometer: it doesn't cure the patient but tells you whether treatment works.

Interview angle. "How do you know your prompt change is an improvement?" → eval with a representative set, paired comparison, regression check.

notes.title: Datasets
notes.html:
Sources.

  • Production samples (anonymized): best match to reality; sample uniformly and oversample failures/edge cases.
  • Expert-authored cases for critical policies, compliance rules, rare but costly scenarios.
  • Synthetic generation: LLM-written variants and adversarial cases; validate quality and diversity; tends to be easier than real traffic.
  • Public benchmarks for sanity checks and comparison, not as the primary measure.
  • Red-team and adversarial sets: jailbreaks, injections, edge inputs.

Composition checklist. Common cases (weighted by frequency), hard/long-tail cases, ambiguous requests, unanswerable/out-of-scope, multi-turn conversations, multiple languages/locales, different user personas, format stress (long, short, messy, empty), safety-sensitive prompts, "should refuse/escalate" and "should not refuse" pairs.

Labelling. Expected output or rubric per case; reference answers where a single correct answer exists; properties to check otherwise (must include X, must not include Y, ≤ N words); metadata tags (category, difficulty, language) for slicing.

Size. 50 to 200 for early development; 500 to 2,000 for mature features; more for fine-grained slices. Statistical power matters: with 100 cases a 5-point difference is often noise.

Hygiene. Version the dataset; keep a frozen test split that isn't used for prompt tuning; avoid duplicates; remove leaked test items from prompts/few-shot examples; refresh with new failures regularly.

Real life. A driving test that includes rain, night and roundabouts, not only an empty road.

notes.title: Graders
notes.html:
Choosing a grader by output type.

Output Grader Strength Weakness
Single label/number Exact match / normalized match cheap, deterministic fails valid paraphrases
Structured/code Code-graded (schema valid, parses, unit tests pass, SQL result equals) objective, cheap doesn't judge quality beyond rules
Short free text with known facts Fact/keyword/semantic match, regex, embedding similarity cheap brittle or shallow
Open-ended quality LLM-as-judge with rubric scalable, handles nuance noisy, biased, costs money
High-stakes / subjective Human review gold standard slow, expensive, also inconsistent

Layer them. Cheap deterministic checks on every run (format, forbidden content, length), LLM judge for quality on every release, humans for periodic calibration and sensitive slices.

Rubric design. Specific criteria with anchored scales (what a 1, 3, 5 looks like), one criterion per question (correctness, completeness, tone, safety), pass/fail per criterion rather than a vague 1 to 10, and instructions to cite evidence.

Real life. Multiple choice is auto-marked; a coding test is run against hidden tests; an essay needs a calibrated examiner.

notes.title: LLM-as-judge done right
notes.html:
Setup. A judge model receives the task, the response(s), optional reference and a rubric, and outputs structured scores with brief reasoning.

Modes.

  • Pointwise (score one response): simple, but scores drift and compress.
  • Pairwise (which is better, A or B): more reliable for relative comparisons; run both orders to cancel position bias.
  • Reference-based: compare to a gold answer (checks correctness).
  • Reference-free: judge against the rubric/context (e.g. faithfulness to retrieved documents).
  • Multi-judge / jury: several models or prompts, aggregate (reduces variance and self-preference).

Known biases and mitigations.

  • Position bias → randomize/swap order.
  • Verbosity bias (prefers longer) → control length or instruct to ignore length; include length-matched cases.
  • Self-preference (favours its own family's style) → use a different judge model family.
  • Sycophancy to the author's claims; leniency (scores cluster high) → anchored rubrics, harder negative examples.
  • Prompt sensitivity → test judge prompt variants.

Calibration protocol.

  1. Collect 50 to 200 outputs labelled by humans (two annotators, measure agreement).
  2. Run the judge; compute agreement (accuracy, Cohen's κ, Spearman for scores) and per-class precision/recall.
  3. Inspect disagreements, refine rubric/prompt, repeat.
  4. Track judge drift when the judge model changes; re-calibrate.
  5. Keep humans in the loop on a sample every cycle.

Cost control. Cheaper judge for screening, stronger judge for ambiguous cases; cache; judge only changed outputs.

Real life. Training the judges at a competition so scores are consistent, and swapping judges to catch favouritism.

notes.title: Metrics and statistics
notes.html:
Choose metrics tied to the product.

  • Classification: accuracy, precision/recall/F1 per class, confusion matrix, cost-weighted error.
  • Generation/QA: correctness, faithfulness/groundedness, completeness, relevance, format validity, citation accuracy.
  • Code: pass@k (at least one of k samples passes), unit-test pass rate.
  • Retrieval: recall@k, MRR, nDCG.
  • Agents: task success, steps, cost, safety violations, pass^k (reliability).
  • Operational: latency percentiles, cost per request, refusal rate, escalation rate, error rate.
  • Safety: attack success rate, harmful output rate, over-refusal rate.

Statistics.

  • Report confidence intervals (bootstrap or Wilson for proportions).
  • Use paired comparisons (same cases for A and B; McNemar or paired bootstrap) — far more sensitive than unpaired.
  • Run multiple samples per case for stochastic systems; separate prompt effect from sampling noise.
  • Beware multiple comparisons (many variants → some win by chance).
  • Report by slice (language, category, difficulty) to uncover hidden regressions; don't rely on a single average.
  • Effect size and practical significance, not only p-values.

Real life. One lucky free throw doesn't make a great shooter.

notes.title: Offline, online and regression testing
notes.html:
Offline evals. Run on fixed datasets before release: development iteration, CI gating, model comparison, red-team suites. Fast and repeatable, but only as representative as the dataset.

Online evaluation.

  • Shadow mode: new version runs on live traffic without user exposure; compare outputs/metrics.
  • Canary release to 1 to 5%.
  • A/B tests on business metrics: resolution rate, task completion, retention, CSAT, revenue; guardrail metrics (latency, cost, safety).
  • Implicit feedback: edits, regenerations, abandonment, escalation, copy actions.
  • Explicit feedback: thumbs, ratings, comments; sampled human review.
  • Production monitoring with automatic graders on sampled traffic to detect drift.

Regression testing. Maintain a suite of previously failing cases and critical behaviours; run in CI on every change of prompt, model version, retrieval config, tools; pin model versions; re-run before provider upgrades; alert on metric drops beyond noise thresholds.

Closed loop. Production failures → triage → add to eval set → fix → verify → deploy.

Real life. Lab tests first, then a pilot with a small group, then full rollout, then ongoing audits.

notes.title: Common eval pitfalls
notes.html:
1. Contamination: test items in prompts, few-shot examples, fine-tuning data, or the model's training set.
  2. Overfitting to the eval: iterating prompts against the same cases until they memorize quirks; keep a frozen test split.
  3. Unrepresentative data: only easy/clean inputs; missing languages and edge cases.
  4. Uncalibrated judges: trusting scores without human agreement checks.
  5. Ignoring variance: single-run comparisons of stochastic systems.
  6. Metric mismatch: optimizing BLEU/ROUGE or length when users care about correctness.
  7. Goodhart effects: the measure becomes the target and stops reflecting quality.
  8. Averaging away failures: a catastrophic safety failure hidden in a high mean.
  9. Eval staleness: product and users change; eval doesn't.
  10. Not reading outputs: numbers hide failure modes; review samples regularly.

Real life. Teaching to the test.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Why evals. Quality must be measurable in a non-deterministic system; write the eval before the feature; iterate with one change at a time; gate releases.

Datasets. Mix production samples, expert cases, synthetic and adversarial; include hard, ambiguous, unanswerable, multilingual and multi-turn cases; label with rubrics/properties and tags; 50 to 200 to start, more for maturity; keep a frozen test split; refresh from failures.

Graders. Exact match (single labels), code checks (structure, tests), semantic/fact matching, LLM-judge (open-ended), humans (gold/high-stakes). Layer them by cost and frequency.

LLM judge. Anchored rubrics, pairwise with order swapping, reference-based when possible, juries, different-family judges; mitigate position, verbosity and self-preference biases; calibrate against human labels (κ, accuracy) and monitor drift.

Metrics/stats. Choose product-aligned metrics, report confidence intervals, use paired tests, slice results, run multiple samples, mind multiple comparisons and practical significance.

Offline + online. CI regression suites; shadow, canary and A/B in production with guardrail metrics; feedback loops; pin model versions.

Pitfalls. Contamination, overfitting, unrepresentative data, uncalibrated judges, variance, Goodhart, averaging away failures, staleness.

Interview one-liners.

  • "No eval, no claim of improvement."
  • "Calibrate the judge against humans before trusting a single number."
  • "Paired comparisons and slices find regressions that averages hide."
  • "Every incident becomes a test case."

questions.promptHtml: What is an "eval" for an LLM application, and why do people say you should build it before the feature?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates engineers who ship on vibes from those who can prove a change helped. It is the foundation of every other answer in this track.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An eval is a fixed set of test cases, each with an expected behaviour, plus a grader that turns the model's output into a score. LLM output is non-deterministic and open-ended, so "looks fine on five examples" proves nothing. If I write the eval first, I can baseline a simple solution, change one thing at a time, and keep or revert based on numbers instead of opinions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Plain words first. A normal unit test says "input 2+2 must give 4". An LLM can answer the same question in a thousand valid ways, and it can silently get worse when you edit the prompt or the provider updates the model. An eval is the LLM version of a test suite: many examples, a scoring rule, one number (or a few) you can compare over time.

The eval-driven loop:

define success criteria -> build dataset + graders -> baseline simple solution
      ^                                                        |
      |                                                        v
 production failures  <-- gate release on eval  <-- change ONE thing -> measure -> keep/revert

Why before the feature: the success criteria force the team to agree on what "good" means; without them, every demo becomes an argument. Also, without a baseline you cannot tell whether a cheaper model or shorter prompt hurt quality.

Expect the first score to be poor (2 to 4 out of 10 is common). The value is the trend and the failure categories you discover, not the first number.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating a handful of hand-picked demos as an eval.
  • Changing prompt, model and retrieval at once, so you cannot attribute the change.
  • Defining "good" as "looks good" instead of gradable criteria.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you know a prompt change is an improvement? → Run both versions on the same representative set, compare paired per-case results with a confidence interval, and check slices for regressions.
  2. Is a bad first score a problem? → No; it gives a baseline and the failure categories to attack.
  3. Who owns the eval? → The feature team; domain experts supply cases and rubrics, and it is gated in CI.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "we test prompts on some examples and see if they look right." Senior: eval-first, one change at a time, paired comparison, release gating, and a closed loop from production failures back into the set.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team swapped to a cheaper model "because the demo looked identical" and only found a 9-point drop on refund questions from customer complaints a week later.

questions.promptHtml: What should go into an eval dataset for a customer-support assistant, and where do the cases come from?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Eval quality is capped by dataset quality. Interviewers want to hear that you cover the long tail and not only the happy path.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I mix sources: anonymized production samples (closest to reality), expert-written cases for policies and costly mistakes, synthetic variants, and adversarial or red-team cases. The set must include common cases weighted by real frequency, plus hard, ambiguous, out-of-scope, multi-turn and multilingual ones. Each case gets an expected answer or a rubric, plus tags like category and language so I can slice results.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A "dataset" here is just a table of inputs with the expectation attached. Sources and their trade-offs:

  • Production samples: best match to real use. Sample uniformly (for the true mix) and then oversample failures and edge cases. Anonymize personal data.
  • Expert-authored: policy and compliance rules, rare but expensive scenarios.
  • Synthetic (LLM-written): cheap variety, but tends to be easier and more uniform than real traffic; validate diversity and quality.
  • Public benchmarks: sanity checks and comparison only; they do not know your product.
  • Red-team sets: jailbreaks, prompt injections, odd formats.

Checklist: common cases, long tail, ambiguous requests, unanswerable questions (the correct output is "I don't know/escalate"), multi-turn chats, other languages, different personas, format stress (empty, very long, messy), safety-sensitive prompts, and matched pairs of "should refuse" and "should not refuse".

Labelling: a reference answer when one exists; otherwise properties (must mention X, must not mention Y, at most N words) or a rubric. Add metadata (category, difficulty, language) for slicing.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only clean, English, single-turn inputs.
  • Synthetic-only data, giving optimistic scores.
  • No negative cases (nothing checks over-refusal or hallucinated answers to unanswerable questions).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How big should it be? → 50 to 200 to start; 500 to 2,000 for mature features, more if you need fine slices.
  2. Why tag cases? → To report per-slice scores and find hidden regressions.
  3. Why include unanswerable questions? → To test that the model abstains instead of inventing an answer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "collect some examples." Senior: stratified by traffic frequency, oversampled failures, adversarial and refusal pairs, tagged for slicing, versioned.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bot scored 94% on a clean English set and failed on code-mixed Hinglish messages that were 18% of real traffic and absent from the set.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide how to grade an LLM output: exact match, code checks, LLM judge, or humans?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you match the grader to the output type and cost, rather than defaulting to "ask GPT to score it".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I pick the cheapest grader that is reliable for the output type. Single labels get exact or normalized match; structured output and code get code-graded checks (schema valid, tests pass); short factual text gets keyword or semantic match; open-ended quality gets an LLM judge with a rubric; high-stakes or subjective slices get humans. I layer them: cheap checks every run, judge each release, humans for calibration.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Output Grader Strength Weakness
Label / number Exact or normalized match cheap, deterministic fails valid paraphrases
JSON / code / SQL Code-graded (parse, schema, unit tests, result equality) objective says nothing about quality beyond rules
Short facts Keyword / regex / embedding similarity cheap brittle or shallow
Open-ended LLM-as-judge with rubric scalable, nuanced noisy, biased, costs money
High stakes Human review gold standard slow, expensive, also inconsistent

Layering example for a support reply: (1) every run, deterministic checks: valid JSON, no forbidden phrases, length limit; (2) every release, an LLM judge scores correctness and tone against a rubric; (3) monthly, humans review a sample and measure judge-vs-human agreement.

Rule of thumb: if you can write the check as code, do. A judge is for what code cannot express.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using an LLM judge where a regex or schema check is exact and free.
  • Using exact match on free text and punishing correct paraphrases.
  • Never checking humans against the automated grader.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not humans for everything? → Slow, costly, and humans disagree with each other too.
  2. How do you grade SQL generation? → Execute it and compare result sets, not strings.
  3. When is embedding similarity a bad grader? → When small differences matter (negation, numbers).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use an LLM to grade." Senior: grader chosen by output type and cost, layered by frequency, with human calibration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A judge was grading JSON validity at roughly $0.002 per case when a three-line schema check would have been free and exact.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between offline and online evaluation, and why do you need both?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know a fixed dataset is only a proxy for real users.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Offline evaluation runs a new version on a fixed dataset before release: fast, repeatable and good for CI gates and model comparison, but only as representative as the dataset. Online evaluation measures real traffic: shadow mode, canary releases, A/B tests on business metrics, and feedback signals. I use offline to filter bad candidates cheaply and online to confirm real-world impact.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Offline: development iteration, CI gating, model comparison, red-team suites. Cheap, no user risk.
  • Shadow mode: new version answers live requests but users never see it; you compare outputs and metrics.
  • Canary: expose 1 to 5% of users; watch guardrail metrics (latency, cost, safety).
  • A/B test: randomize users, measure business outcomes such as resolution rate, task completion, retention, CSAT.
  • Implicit feedback: edits, regenerations, abandonment, escalation, copy actions. Explicit: thumbs, ratings, comments.
  • Automatic graders on sampled traffic detect drift.

Analogy: lab test, small pilot, full rollout, then ongoing audits. Offline answers "is it likely better?"; online answers "did users actually benefit?".

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Shipping to 100% on an offline win alone.
  • Reading thumbs-up rates without noting that only a few percent of users click them.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why shadow before canary? → It exposes behaviour on real inputs with zero user risk.
  2. Name a guardrail metric. → Latency p95, cost per request, safety violation rate.
  3. Why can offline and online disagree? → The dataset misses part of real traffic or the metric is not what users value.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "test then deploy." Senior: staged exposure with guardrails and a feedback loop that turns failures into new offline cases.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A model improved offline accuracy by 4 points but the canary showed a 12% rise in escalations because answers got longer and less actionable.

questions.promptHtml: Design the graders for a feature that extracts invoice fields into JSON. What do you check in code, what needs a rubric, and how do you write a good rubric?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical grader design: deterministic first, rubric for the rest, with anchored criteria.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For structured output I grade in code: valid JSON, schema conforms, each field equals the gold value after normalization (dates, currency). Only things code cannot judge, like whether a free-text summary is faithful, get a rubric. A good rubric has one criterion per question, anchored descriptions of what each level looks like, pass/fail per criterion instead of a vague 1 to 10, and a request to cite evidence.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per-field scoring beats whole-object match: one wrong field should not zero out nine right ones, and per-field accuracy shows which field is weak. Normalize before comparing ("1,200.00" vs "1200"; "03/04/2025" vs ISO date), otherwise you punish formatting, not correctness.

Rubric example for a summary field:

Criterion: faithfulness (pass/fail)
 PASS: every claim is supported by the invoice text.
 FAIL: any amount, date or party not in the invoice text.
Return: {"faithful": true/false, "evidence": "<quote>"}

Anchors ("what a fail looks like") make a judge, or a human, consistent. Separate criteria (correctness, completeness, tone, safety) so one score does not blur them.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import json

def grade(raw: str, gold: dict) -> dict:
    try:
        out = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {"valid": False, "field_acc": 0.0}
    hits = sum(str(out.get(k)).strip() == str(v).strip() for k, v in gold.items())
    return {"valid": True, "field_acc": hits / len(gold)}
// Uses Jackson (com.fasterxml.jackson.module:jackson-module-kotlin)
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper

fun grade(raw: String, gold: Map<String, String>): Pair<Boolean, Double> {
    val node = try { ObjectMapper().readTree(raw) } catch (e: Exception) { return false to 0.0 }
    val hits = gold.count { (k, v) -> node.path(k).asText().trim() == v.trim() }
    return true to hits.toDouble() / gold.size
}
// Uses Jackson (com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind)
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.*;
import java.util.Map;

static double fieldAcc(String raw, Map<String, String> gold) {
    JsonNode node;
    try { node = new ObjectMapper().readTree(raw); } catch (Exception e) { return 0.0; }
    long hits = gold.entrySet().stream()
        .filter(e -> node.path(e.getKey()).asText().trim().equals(e.getValue().trim())).count();
    return (double) hits / gold.size();
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Whole-object exact match (too harsh, hides which field fails).
  • A 1 to 10 scale with no anchors; judges cluster around 7 to 8.
  • Forgetting to normalize formats before comparing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why pass/fail per criterion? → Easier to apply consistently and to aggregate.
  2. How do you handle optional fields? → Gold stores null; grade "absent" as correct, "hallucinated value" as an error.
  3. How do you stop a judge from being lenient? → Anchors with failing examples and harder negatives in the calibration set.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "compare JSON to expected." Senior: per-field metrics with normalization, validity tracked separately, rubric only where code cannot decide.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's extraction eval reported 61% because dates compared as raw strings; after normalization the true score was 88% and the real weak field (tax id) became visible.

questions.promptHtml: Explain LLM-as-judge: the main modes, the known biases, and how you mitigate each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Judges are everywhere and are routinely trusted blindly. Interviewers look for bias awareness and concrete mitigations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LLM judge is a model given the task, one or more responses, optionally a reference answer, and a rubric, and it returns structured scores with a short reason. Modes: pointwise (score one), pairwise (A vs B, more reliable for relative comparison), reference-based (check against gold) and reference-free (judge against context). Biases: position, verbosity, self-preference and leniency. I mitigate by swapping order, controlling length, using a different model family, and anchored rubrics.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Pointwise: simple but scores drift and compress toward the middle or top.
  • Pairwise: "which is better?" is easier for a model than "give an absolute number"; run both orders (A,B) and (B,A) and count only consistent verdicts, treating inconsistent ones as ties.
  • Reference-based: compares to a gold answer, good for correctness. Reference-free: checks faithfulness to retrieved documents, tone, rule compliance.
  • Jury: several judges (models or prompts), aggregate; reduces variance and self-preference.

Biases:

Bias Meaning Mitigation
Position prefers first (or second) answer randomize / swap order
Verbosity prefers longer text instruct to ignore length, include length-matched cases
Self-preference favours its own family's style judge from a different family
Leniency scores cluster high anchored rubric, hard negatives
Prompt sensitivity verdict changes with wording test judge prompt variants

Output a structured verdict (JSON with reason then score) so parsing is deterministic.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Single-order pairwise comparisons.
  • Using the same model as generator and judge and reporting a big win.
  • Free-text verdicts parsed with regex.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is pairwise more reliable? → Relative judgments are easier than calibrated absolute scores.
  2. Does asking for reasoning first help? → Often yes for consistency, but verify on your calibration set.
  3. How do you detect verbosity bias? → Check the correlation between judge score and length on human-rated data.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use GPT as a judge." Senior: names biases, swaps order, uses cross-family judges, and validates against humans.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An A/B of two prompts showed a 70% judge win rate for the new one; swapping order dropped it to 54%, and most of the "win" was position bias.

questions.contextHtml: Your team has 100 labelled test cases for a classification prompt. Prompt A scores 78/100 and prompt B scores 83/100. The PM says "B is 5 points better, ship it". Each case was run once at temperature 0.7. The two prompts were run on the same 100 cases. Eng lead asks whether this is real.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond, and what would you do before shipping?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "5 points is 5 points, B wins." It ignores sampling noise, small n, and the fact that a single stochastic run was used.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 5-point gap worth the cost increase? (practical significance). Are the 100 cases representative? Is any prompt change confounded with a model change? Is a regression on a critical slice acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not ship yet; this is a decision, not an outage, so nothing to roll back.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the gap is noise (a 95% interval on a proportion near 0.8 with n=100 is about plus or minus 8 points), (b) sampling noise from temperature 0.7, (c) B is truly better on some slices and worse on others, (d) B is better but the effect is small.
  4. How I'd verify each: Paired comparison on the same cases: count discordant pairs (A right/B wrong vs A wrong/B right) and run McNemar or a paired bootstrap. Rerun 3 to 5 samples per case, or at temperature 0, to separate prompt from sampling noise. Slice by category.
  5. Root cause: With n=100, 5 points is often within noise; unpaired reasoning wastes the pairing.
  6. Fix: Grow the set to 500+ for decisions that matter, report the difference with a confidence interval, and decide on the interval plus cost.
  7. Prevention: A standard eval report template: CI, paired test, slice table, cost.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not chase significance by adding cases that favour B; I would not run twenty prompt variants and pick the winner without correcting for multiple comparisons.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Discordant pairs are 9 vs 4. Significant? → Exact McNemar on 13 discordant pairs gives p about 0.27, not convincing.
  • B costs 3x more. → Then I need a clearly practical gain, not just a statistical one.
  • Can you shrink the noise cheaply? → Yes, multiple samples per case and paired analysis.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A prompt "won" by 6 points on 120 cases; after rerunning with five samples each, the gap fell to 1.2 points with an interval straddling zero. The team saved a costly model migration.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the 5-point difference at face value.
  • Hire: mentions confidence intervals and paired testing.
  • Strong hire: also quantifies the interval, separates sampling noise, handles slices, and weighs cost and practical significance.

questions.promptHtml: You built an LLM judge. How do you prove it is trustworthy before using its scores to make decisions?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common eval failure is an uncalibrated judge. They want the protocol, not the slogan.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I calibrate it against humans. I collect 50 to 200 outputs labelled by two annotators, measure how well the humans agree with each other, run the judge, and compute agreement with the human consensus using accuracy, Cohen's kappa (agreement beyond chance) and per-class precision and recall. Then I read the disagreements, fix the rubric, and repeat. I recalibrate whenever the judge model changes and keep a human sample in every cycle.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Accuracy alone misleads when classes are imbalanced: if 90% of outputs are "good", a judge that always says "good" is 90% accurate. Cohen's kappa corrects for chance agreement: kappa = (po - pe) / (1 - pe), where po is observed agreement and pe is the agreement expected by chance. Rough guide: above 0.6 is substantial, above 0.8 is strong (conventions vary). For numeric scores use rank correlation (Spearman).

Human agreement is the ceiling: if two annotators only reach kappa 0.5, a judge cannot be expected to exceed that, and the rubric is probably ambiguous.

Steps:

  1. Sample outputs, including hard ones, and have 2 humans label them.
  2. Resolve conflicts, producing a gold label.
  3. Run the judge; compute accuracy, kappa, precision/recall for the "bad" class (usually what matters).
  4. Read every disagreement and classify the cause (rubric vague, judge bias, label error).
  5. Update the rubric or prompt; re-run; freeze a version.
  6. Re-check periodically for drift.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed; the metric is a few lines of arithmetic over a 2x2 table and every stats library has cohen_kappa_score.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.
  • Calibrating on easy outputs only.
  • Tuning the rubric on the same labelled set used to report agreement (overfitting the judge).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if humans disagree a lot? → Fix the rubric; the task is under-specified.
  2. Which class's recall matters? → Usually "bad" outputs: a judge that misses failures gives false comfort.
  3. When do you recalibrate? → On judge model change, rubric change, or distribution shift.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "I spot-checked a few and it seemed right." Senior: dual annotation, kappa, per-class metrics, held-out calibration split, and drift tracking.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A judge reached 92% accuracy but kappa 0.31 because nearly everything was "pass"; it was missing most real failures.

questions.promptHtml: How do you compare two prompt versions statistically, and why are paired comparisons better than unpaired ones?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates compare means. Seniors report uncertainty and exploit pairing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I run both versions on the same cases and compare per-case results. That is a paired design: it removes case difficulty from the noise, so it detects much smaller differences than comparing two separate averages. I report the difference with a bootstrap confidence interval, and for pass/fail data I can use McNemar's test on the discordant pairs. I also report effect size, not only p-values.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Some cases are easy for both versions, others hard for both. Unpaired comparison treats that case-difficulty spread as noise. Paired comparison looks only at the per-case difference d_i = score_B - score_A. If most d_i are 0 and a few are +1 or -1, the signal is in those few.

Bootstrap: resample the per-case differences with replacement many times (say 10,000), compute the mean each time, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the 95% interval. If it excludes 0, the difference is unlikely to be noise. For a single proportion, a Wilson interval is better than the naive normal approximation at small n.

Also: stochastic systems need several samples per case so you separate prompt effect from sampling noise; and with many variants tested, some win by chance (multiple comparisons).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = np.array(scores_b) - np.array(scores_a)          # per-case paired differences
boots = [rng.choice(d, size=len(d), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(10_000)]
print(d.mean(), np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5]))
import kotlin.random.Random

fun bootstrapCi(d: DoubleArray, iters: Int = 10_000, seed: Int = 0): Pair<Double, Double> {
    val rnd = Random(seed)
    val means = DoubleArray(iters) { DoubleArray(d.size) { d[rnd.nextInt(d.size)] }.average() }
    means.sort()
    return means[(iters * 0.025).toInt()] to means[(iters * 0.975).toInt()]
}
import java.util.*;

static double[] bootstrapCi(double[] d, int iters, long seed) {
    Random rnd = new Random(seed);
    double[] means = new double[iters];
    for (int i = 0; i < iters; i++) {
        double s = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < d.length; j++) s += d[rnd.nextInt(d.length)];
        means[i] = s / d.length;
    }
    Arrays.sort(means);
    return new double[]{means[(int) (iters * 0.025)], means[(int) (iters * 0.975)]};
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting two averages with no uncertainty.
  • Using an unpaired test on paired data (wastes power).
  • Ignoring that 100 cases give wide intervals.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is Wilson better than normal? → Small n or proportions near 0 or 1.
  2. What does McNemar use? → Only the discordant pairs (A right/B wrong vs A wrong/B right).
  3. Does a significant p-value mean it is worth shipping? → No; check effect size, cost and slice regressions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "B scored higher." Senior: paired bootstrap interval, effect size, multiple-sample runs, slice breakdown.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team re-ran an "improvement" with a paired interval of -1.5 to +3.0 points; they stopped a model migration with no evidence of gain.

questions.contextHtml: A RAG question-answering prompt scored 96% on the eval set last month. After launch, users report roughly 70% helpfulness and support tickets mention wrong answers. A review finds that the prompt's few-shot examples were copied from the eval set, 14 of the 150 eval cases appear verbatim in the prompt, and the team had tuned the prompt 40 times against these same cases. Nobody noticed because the number kept going up.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, and how do you repair the eval process?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more test cases." It misses that the held-out property was destroyed, and that a bigger set tuned against repeatedly has the same problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was there ever a frozen split? How were the 14 examples chosen? Is the production sample drawn from the same distribution? Do the dev cases include the production failures?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the leaked cases from the prompt (or from the eval), re-score, and communicate that the 96% is not valid.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) direct leakage (few-shot copies), (b) overfitting through 40 rounds of tuning on the same cases, (c) dataset unrepresentative of live traffic, (d) retrieval quality differs in production.
  4. How I'd verify each: Exact and fuzzy match prompt text against eval inputs; evaluate on a fresh sample of 200 production queries labelled by experts; compare the dev vs fresh scores; check a retrieval recall metric separately.
  5. Root cause: Contamination plus repeated tuning on a visible set. The eval stopped measuring generalization and became a training signal.
  6. Fix: Rebuild into a dev set (iterate freely) and a frozen test set (touched only at release decisions); add a dedup check in CI that fails if any eval input appears in prompts or few-shot examples; refresh the test set from new production failures.
  7. Prevention: Dataset versioning, a contamination lint, a rule that few-shot examples come from a separate pool, periodic fresh-sample audits.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not simply discard the old set (it still has regression value); and I would not rely only on a bigger synthetic set, which may be easier than real traffic.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The fresh set scores 74%. Is the model bad? → Possibly the true level; compare with the baseline on the same fresh set to judge progress.
  • Can a fine-tuning set leak the same way? → Yes; dedupe training data against eval data.
  • How often to refresh the frozen set? → Every few weeks with new failures, retiring items that became stale.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team found that a marketing demo question was in the prompt and in the eval; the "perfect" score on it drove a launch decision. A fresh sample showed a 22-point gap.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests only adding more cases.
  • Hire: identifies contamination and overfitting and proposes a frozen split.
  • Strong hire: adds a CI contamination lint, fresh production audit, versioning and a process rule separating dev and test usage.

questions.promptHtml: What metrics would you choose for a classifier, a RAG answerer, a code generator and an agent? Explain pass@k versus pass^k.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Metric choice shows product thinking. The pass@k versus pass^k distinction shows depth about reliability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Metrics follow the product. Classifiers: per-class precision, recall, F1, a confusion matrix, and cost-weighted error. RAG answers: correctness, faithfulness to retrieved text, completeness, and citation accuracy, with retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR, nDCG) reported separately. Code: unit-test pass rate and pass@k. Agents: task success, steps, cost, safety violations, and pass^k. pass@k asks "did at least one of k tries succeed" (good for brainstorming/search); pass^k asks "did all k tries succeed" (reliability, what users feel).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
pass@k: if single-try success probability is p, the chance that at least one of k tries succeeds is 1 - (1-p)^k. With p = 0.6 and k = 5, pass@5 is about 0.99. pass^k: the chance that all k succeed is p^k. With p = 0.6, pass^5 is about 0.08. For a customer-facing agent that must work every time, the second number is the honest one.

Operational metrics matter too: latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), cost per request, refusal rate, escalation rate, error rate. Safety: attack success rate, harmful output rate, over-refusal rate.

Report these by slice (language, category, difficulty) because a single mean hides weakness.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed; formulas above are the content. In a notebook it is 1 - (1-p)**k and p**k.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting accuracy for a heavily imbalanced classification problem.
  • Reporting pass@k for a user-facing agent that has to succeed on one attempt.
  • Judging RAG by final answer only, so you cannot tell retrieval failures from generation failures.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why separate retrieval and generation metrics? → To localize the failure.
  2. What does MRR measure? → The reciprocal rank of the first relevant result, averaged.
  3. Why track over-refusal? → Safety fixes can make the model uselessly cautious.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "accuracy and BLEU." Senior: metrics tied to user impact, reliability measures (pass^k), cost and latency guardrails, and slices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An agent had 82% single-run success but pass^5 of 37%, which matched the "it works sometimes" complaints.

questions.contextHtml: After a prompt update, the weekly eval dashboard shows overall quality went from 88.4% to 89.1%, so the release went out. Two days later a Spanish-language support queue shows a spike: complaints up from 40 to 190 per day. Spanish is 8% of traffic. Looking at the data, English improved from 90.2% to 91.8%, while Spanish dropped from 79% to 61%. The headline metric moved up.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why the dashboard missed this, and what you change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back and add Spanish tests", without explaining the averaging problem or building a gate that would have caught it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many Spanish cases were in the eval (a handful makes the slice noisy)? Does the prompt contain English-only instructions? Which other languages exist in traffic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back, or route Spanish traffic to the previous prompt version via a feature flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) averaged metric hid a slice regression (8% of traffic x -18 points = about -1.4 overall, offset by English gains), (b) English-only formatting rule in the new prompt, (c) tokenization/translation side effects, (d) the Spanish eval slice is too small to see it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute per-slice scores with confidence intervals; read 30 failed Spanish outputs; diff the old and new prompts; check the count of Spanish cases (for a 61% score, 40 cases gives an interval of roughly plus or minus 15).
  5. Root cause: Reporting a single mean with a small Spanish slice and no per-slice release gate.
  6. Fix: Fix the prompt, then re-evaluate with at least 100 Spanish cases and per-slice thresholds.
  7. Prevention: Gate on both the overall score and minimum per-slice scores (no slice drops more than 2 to 3 points beyond noise); tag every case with language, category and difficulty.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Many slices increase false alarms (multiple comparisons), so use meaningful thresholds and larger samples for important slices; I would not add dozens of tiny slices with ten cases each.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Spanish slice has only 12 cases. → Too small to gate; grow it, and meanwhile use online monitoring.
  • Should safety be averaged with quality? → No; a catastrophic safety failure must be its own hard gate.
  • Is a macro-average better? → It can protect small slices, but pick it deliberately and also show per-slice values.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A summarizer improvement passed on the average but broke on documents above 20 pages, 5% of traffic but the highest-value customers; a length slice had been missing.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the Spanish team or only rolls back.
  • Hire: identifies averaging and proposes slice reporting.
  • Strong hire: adds sizing of slices, confidence intervals, per-slice release gates and live monitoring.

questions.promptHtml: How do you build regression testing for an LLM application, and what triggers it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: LLM apps break silently when a model, prompt or retrieval setting changes. They want to hear a CI mindset.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A regression suite is a set of previously failing cases and critical behaviours that must not break. I run it in CI on every change to prompts, model versions, retrieval config or tools; I pin model versions so the provider cannot change behaviour underneath me; I re-run before any provider upgrade; and I alert when a metric drops beyond a noise threshold. Every production incident becomes a new test case.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Triggers: prompt edit, model or version switch, embedding model or chunking change, retrieval parameters, tool schema changes, library upgrades, and a scheduled run (provider-side drift on unpinned aliases).

Design:

  • Fast tier (minutes, runs on every PR): a small deterministic subset of 50 to 200 cases, mostly code-graded.
  • Full tier (nightly or pre-release): the whole dataset with a judge.
  • Noise-aware thresholds: because outputs vary, fail the build when a drop exceeds what repeated runs would show (for example more than 3 points, or a paired interval excluding zero), not on any decrease.
  • Pinned versions: use dated model identifiers rather than moving aliases so results are reproducible (verify what your provider offers).

Closed loop: production failure, triage, add to the set, fix, verify, deploy.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running evals only manually before big launches.
  • Failing CI on tiny drops that are inside noise, leading the team to ignore the gate.
  • Using a floating "latest" model alias.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep CI affordable? → Fast code-graded tier on PRs, judge-based tier nightly, cache unchanged outputs.
  2. What if the test is flaky? → Multiple samples and a tolerance band, or temperature 0 for the fast tier.
  3. What to do when the provider deprecates a model? → Run the full suite on the replacement, compare paired, then migrate via canary.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "we have some tests." Senior: tiered suites, noise-aware gates, pinned versions, incident-to-test loop.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A silent alias update changed output format slightly and broke a downstream parser; no test noticed for 3 days.

questions.contextHtml:
A team compares a new prompt (candidate) against the current one (baseline) with a pairwise judge. It reports "candidate wins 68% of 200 comparisons". Reviewers are suspicious because the candidate's answers are only slightly longer. Here is the harness:

def compare(question, baseline_ans, candidate_ans, judge):
    # judge(question, a, b) -> "A" or "B"
    verdict = judge(question, baseline_ans, candidate_ans)
    return verdict == "B"        # candidate wins

Re-running the same data with the arguments reversed gives the candidate only 49% wins.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The judge is noisy, use a better judge." It misses that the harness always places the candidate second, so position bias is baked in.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the judge allow ties? How was the judge validated? Are lengths matched?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Withdraw the 68% claim.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fixed position (candidate always B) and the judge prefers the second answer, (b) verbosity bias, (c) real quality gain, (d) self-preference.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run both orders on all 200 pairs and count consistent wins, losses and inconsistent verdicts; compute judge score vs length correlation; test with a judge of a different family.
  5. Root cause: The harness always sends candidate as B. A judge with a 19-point lean toward B produced a spurious win.
  6. Fix: Evaluate both orders and count a win only when both agree; otherwise call it a tie.
  7. Prevention: Make order swapping the default in the harness, log position-consistency rate, and fail the report if the inconsistency rate exceeds a threshold.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Doubling judge calls doubles cost; I would reduce cost via a cheaper judge screening, not drop swapping.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def compare(q, base, cand, judge):
    r1 = judge(q, base, cand)      # candidate is B
    r2 = judge(q, cand, base)      # candidate is A
    cand_wins = (r1 == "B") + (r2 == "A")
    return "win" if cand_wins == 2 else "loss" if cand_wins == 0 else "tie"
fun compare(q: String, base: String, cand: String, judge: (String, String, String) -> String): String {
    val wins = (if (judge(q, base, cand) == "B") 1 else 0) +
               (if (judge(q, cand, base) == "A") 1 else 0)
    return when (wins) { 2 -> "win"; 0 -> "loss"; else -> "tie" }
}
import java.util.function.Function;

interface Judge { String apply(String q, String a, String b); }

static String compare(String q, String base, String cand, Judge judge) {
    int wins = (judge.apply(q, base, cand).equals("B") ? 1 : 0)
             + (judge.apply(q, cand, base).equals("A") ? 1 : 0);
    return wins == 2 ? "win" : wins == 0 ? "loss" : "tie";
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• After the fix, wins are 41%, losses 30%, ties 29%. Ship? → A paired interval on win minus loss is needed; 11-point margin with 200 cases is borderline, so check CI and human spot checks.
  • Judge returns "tie" often. → Acceptable; it carries information.
  • Randomizing order per case instead of both? → Fine on average, but both orders gives per-case consistency data.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's dashboard showed gains for six consecutive weeks; the cause was the harness placing new outputs second.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames judge noise.
  • Hire: finds fixed ordering and proposes swapping.
  • Strong hire: counts consistent verdicts only, reports consistency rate, and cross-checks with different judge and humans.

questions.promptHtml: What is Goodhart's law in evals, and how do you stop a team from optimizing the metric instead of quality?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers know that a metric which becomes a target stops measuring what it measured.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Goodhart's law says when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. In evals this shows as prompts tuned until they exploit judge quirks, length inflation because judges like long answers, or memorizing eval items. I defend with a frozen test split used rarely, several complementary metrics, regular reading of raw outputs, fresh production samples, human audits, and guardrail metrics that catch the trade-offs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Every iteration on a visible set leaks a little information from it into the prompt, so after dozens of rounds the score no longer predicts live performance (overfitting to the eval). Metric gaming is a related effect: if the judge rewards confident-sounding long answers, optimization finds those; if you optimize ROUGE you get answers that overlap the reference words but may be wrong.

Defenses:

  • Splits: dev set for tuning, frozen test set for release decisions; track how often the test set is read.
  • Metric portfolio: quality plus length, cost, refusal rate, latency, so gaming one shows damage in another.
  • Fresh data: periodically evaluate on new production samples and compare dev vs fresh scores; a growing gap signals overfitting.
  • Read outputs: numbers hide failure modes; sample 20 to 50 outputs per release.
  • Human audits of the judge on a rotating sample.

Also watch the opposite failure, averaging away a rare catastrophic failure inside a high mean.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting the same set's score over many iterations as progress.
  • Single metric dashboards.
  • Never reading raw outputs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you detect eval overfitting? → Dev-vs-fresh gap widens over time.
  2. Example of metric gaming with a judge? → Answers grow longer while users read less.
  3. How do you handle safety? → Separate hard gate, never averaged into a quality score.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "keep improving the score." Senior: protects the measurement itself with splits, portfolios, fresh data, and human audits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's helpfulness score rose 12 points in a quarter while average answer length doubled and user satisfaction stayed flat.

questions.contextHtml: You run a nightly judge-based eval over 1,500 cases using judge model J1 from the same family as your production generator. The provider announces J1 retires in 30 days; you switch the judge to J2. Same outputs, same rubric: the average score moves from 4.3 to 3.7 out of 5, and the "faithfulness pass rate" drops from 91% to 78%. Product leadership asks if quality fell by 13 points. No generator change has shipped this week.
questions.promptHtml: How do you handle this, and how do you keep history comparable?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "J2 is stricter, ignore it" or "quality dropped, roll back" without evidence either way.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which outputs were scored by both judges? Did the rubric text or output schema change? Was J1 the same family as the generator (self-preference)? Do we have human labels?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Tell leadership the drop is a measurement change until proven otherwise; hold the dashboards and do not roll back.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) J2 is stricter or differently calibrated, (b) J1 had self-preference inflating scores, (c) rubric parsing differs on J2, (d) real regression (unlikely, nothing shipped).
  4. How I'd verify each: Score the same 1,500 outputs with both judges and compare the per-case agreement and confusion table; score a 150-case human-labelled calibration set with each judge and compute kappa and precision/recall for the failure class; read 30 disagreements.
  5. Root cause: Two judges have different calibrations; the old 91% was partly self-preference and leniency, which the stricter J2 corrected (if humans agree with J2).
  6. Fix: Pick the judge with better agreement with humans; re-run the last 4 to 8 weeks of stored outputs with the new judge to rebuild a comparable history; document the version change on the dashboard.
  7. Prevention: Version judge and rubric in the report; always keep an overlap period running both judges; use a different family than the generator; recalibrate on every judge change.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Overlap runs cost double for a few weeks; I would not apply a fixed "correction factor", as the shift differs by slice.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Humans side with J1. → Then J2's rubric interpretation is off; tune the prompt or keep J1 via a pinned alternative.
  • You can't re-score old outputs. → Keep only the overlap period as the bridge and annotate the discontinuity.
  • Use both? → A jury of both reduces variance, at higher cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team discovered months later that a 6-point "improvement" coincided exactly with a silent judge-model update, not with any prompt change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the 13-point drop as real or ignores it.
  • Hire: recognizes the judge change and suggests overlap/human checking.
  • Strong hire: re-scores history, uses kappa on human labels, versions judges, and mentions self-preference.

questions.subtopic: Building a dataset from scratch with synthetic data
questions.promptHtml: You have no production traffic yet. How would you bootstrap an eval dataset, and what are the dangers of using an LLM to generate it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cold-start eval design is common at startups. They want a plan that avoids over-optimistic synthetic data.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start with a small seed set written by domain experts (50 to 100 cases) that covers the critical policies, then use an LLM to expand it with variants, paraphrases and adversarial cases. I validate the synthetic cases by human sampling, check diversity, and tag provenance. The danger is that synthetic data is cleaner and easier than real traffic and shares the generator's biases, so I replace it with real production samples as soon as they exist and never use it as the only measure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Steps:

  1. Define scenarios from the product spec: personas, intents, failure modes, languages.
  2. Seed with experts (or design partners): they provide hard, realistic cases.
  3. Generate variants with an LLM, using a structured template per scenario (persona, intent, tone, length, typos) so you do not get 200 near duplicates.
  4. Filter: dedupe by embedding similarity, remove cases the model finds trivial, and human-check a random 10 to 20%.
  5. Label: expected answers or rubrics written or verified by humans; do not let the same model that will be evaluated generate the gold answers unchecked.
  6. Tag each case as synthetic vs real, so you can compare score gaps later.
  7. Replace with production data once available (dogfooding, beta users).

Dangers: easier distribution (scores inflated), low diversity, shared bias with the system under test, and gold labels containing the generator's mistakes.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the same model to generate cases and answers and then declaring it passes.
  • Hundreds of near-identical paraphrases counted as coverage.
  • Never refreshing with real data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you measure diversity? → Embedding clustering, coverage of tags, nearest-neighbour similarity distribution.
  2. How do you check synthetic vs real difficulty? → Compare scores on both; synthetic is usually higher.
  3. Can synthetic data be used for red-teaming? → Yes, adversarial generation is a strong use case.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "ask GPT to generate 500 test questions." Senior: expert seed, structured generation, filtering, human verification, provenance tags, and migration to real traffic.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup's synthetic set scored 93%, while the first week of real users yielded 71% because users sent short, typo-filled, multi-intent messages.

questions.contextHtml: A new summarization prompt beats the old one offline: judge score 4.1 vs 3.8 on 600 cases (paired CI +0.15 to +0.45), and cost per request is the same. A 5% canary for a week (about 40,000 users each arm) shows: summary copy actions down 9%, regeneration clicks up 14%, thumbs-up unchanged, and latency p95 up from 2.1s to 2.6s. Leadership wants to know whether to ship.
questions.promptHtml: How do you decide, and what do you investigate?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Offline is stronger statistically, ship." Or "Online wins, trust users." Both skip diagnosing why the signals disagree.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the canary randomized by user? Which metric is the product's primary success measure? Is the 9% change significant with a CI? Did the average output length change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hold at 5%; do not expand.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the new prompt produces longer summaries that the judge likes (verbosity) but users do not (more regenerations, slower), (b) offline set under-represents real input types, (c) latency harm reduces satisfaction, (d) novelty effect or noise.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare output length distributions; correlate judge scores with length; split online metrics by input type; compare the production input distribution to the offline set; run the A/B for another week; sample 50 summaries from each arm for human review.
  5. Root cause (likely): Judge rewarded thoroughness, the product values brevity and speed; offline metric mismatch with the user's goal.
  6. Fix: Add a length/conciseness criterion to the rubric, re-baseline with human labels reflecting user preference, add a latency guardrail, and retest.
  7. Prevention: Put online-linked metrics (copy rate, regeneration rate) into the offline evaluation by correlating them; define guardrail metrics before the test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not override business metrics with an offline judge score; I would not stop the canary early unless a safety guardrail trips.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Everything is flat except latency. → Latency is a cost; reject unless quality gain is visible to users.
  • Offline and online agree but humans dislike both. → Revisit the success definition.
  • Sample ratio mismatch (arms of unequal size)? → Suspect a bug in assignment; the result is invalid.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's "better" answers added three disclaimers; the judge loved the caution, users hit regenerate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one side.
  • Hire: identifies metric mismatch and proposes more analysis.
  • Strong hire: ties judge to user behaviour, uses guardrail metrics, checks significance and randomization, and iterates on the eval itself.

questions.promptHtml: You test 20 prompt variants and the best one beats the baseline by 4 points. Is that a real win? How should you run such a search?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This tests understanding of winner's curse and selection bias, which is a staple of senior experimentation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Not necessarily. If you try 20 variants on the same data, the best one tends to look good partly by luck (the winner's curse), so its measured gain overstates its true gain. I treat the search set as dev data, then confirm the top one or two on a fresh held-out set with a paired comparison and an interval, and I report how many variants were tried.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Plain words: each score has noise. Take 20 noisy numbers around the same true value and the maximum will be above average just by chance. With a 95% threshold per comparison and 20 comparisons, the chance that at least one variant looks "significant" with no real effect is 1 - 0.95^20, about 64%.

Process:

  1. Run the search on a dev set; use several samples per case to reduce sampling noise.
  2. Shortlist the top candidates.
  3. Confirm on the frozen test set once, paired against baseline, with a confidence interval.
  4. Apply a correction when making formal claims (Bonferroni or false-discovery-rate control), or simply require the effect to hold on fresh data.
  5. Report the effect size and cost, not just "significant".

Cheaper search: successive halving (evaluate many variants on a small subset, keep the best half, and increase evaluation size).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting the best of N on the same data used to pick it.
  • Not recording the number of variants tried.
  • Treating tiny improvements as meaningful.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the winner's curse? → The selected maximum overestimates its true value.
  2. What does a held-out confirmation do? → Gives an unbiased estimate of the chosen variant.
  3. Is Bonferroni always right? → It is conservative; FDR methods trade a bit more power.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "pick the highest score." Senior: understands selection bias, confirms on fresh data, controls for multiple comparisons.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An optimizer-generated prompt gained 5 points on dev data and 0.8 on the frozen set.

questions.contextHtml: You join a team building an HR-policy assistant for 12,000 employees; launch is in 8 weeks. Stakeholders say "it should be accurate and safe" and nothing else. There is no data yet, only 40 policy PDFs. Legal worries about wrong answers on leave and compensation. Budget for human review is about 20 hours per week from two HR experts. Daily traffic is estimated at 3,000 questions.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out the evaluation plan from day one to launch and the first month after.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Collect some questions and test them." No success criteria, no grader plan, no gating, no post-launch loop.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What counts as a critical error (wrong leave entitlement)? What is acceptable failure rate per category? Should it refuse out-of-scope questions or escalate? Which languages? What is the escalation path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Pre-launch, so framing instead) agree success criteria in writing: for example 95% correctness on top policy categories, 0 tolerated confident wrong answers on legal-sensitive topics, abstain-or-escalate when unsure.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) hallucinated policy details, (b) retrieval misses the right document, (c) outdated policy versions, (d) over-refusal making it useless, (e) personal data leakage.
  4. How I'd verify each: Weeks 1 to 2: HR experts write 100 seed questions with reference answers and policy citations; generate 300 synthetic variants and human-check a sample; weeks 2 to 4: build code-graded checks (citation present and pointing to the right doc), LLM judge for faithfulness against retrieved text, calibrated against 150 expert labels (kappa); separate retrieval metrics (recall@k) from answer metrics.
  5. Root cause (of risk): Wrong answers in a legal domain are costly; the gate must reflect that cost.
  6. Fix (launch gates): Frozen test set with per-category thresholds; red-team set for injection and privacy; unanswerable cases that must abstain; weeks 6 to 8: shadow mode on pilot teams, expert review of 100 sampled answers per week.
  7. Prevention: After launch: canary, log thumbs and escalations, auto-grade a 5% sample, weekly triage turns failures into new cases, pin model versions, regression suite in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not spend expert time labelling everything; they calibrate the judge and review high-risk slices. I would not launch broadly before a pilot.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Policy changes monthly. → Version the corpus and eval; add a freshness test for changed policies.
  • Experts disagree on an answer. → That is a policy ambiguity; resolve with HR owners before it becomes the gold label.
  • Traffic is multilingual. → Add language tags and per-language thresholds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A policy bot passed all synthetic tests but cited a superseded leave policy; a "policy version" field in the dataset and a staleness test fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: vague testing plan.
  • Hire: dataset, graders, gates and post-launch monitoring.
  • Strong hire: explicit success criteria, expert time budgeting, calibration, abstention testing, staged rollout and incident-to-test loop.

questions.contextHtml: You run an automatic quality grader on production traffic. Volume is 2 million responses per day; each judge call uses about 1,800 input tokens (task, response, context, rubric) and 150 output tokens. Judging everything with a frontier model costs about the equivalent of a mid-size engineering budget (check the provider's current prices; call it $9 per 1M input tokens and $45 per 1M output tokens for the illustration, which is made-up for the arithmetic). Finance asks you to cut spend by 90% without losing the ability to detect regressions.
questions.promptHtml: How do you do it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a cheaper model for everything" with no validation, or "sample 1%" with no thought about rare problems.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What decisions does this score feed (alerts, release gates, reports)? What is the acceptable detection delay? Which failure types are rare but critical?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop judging the whole stream; lower to a sample while redesigning.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (cost levers): (a) sampling, (b) cheap deterministic prefilters, (c) cheap judge screening plus strong judge on ambiguous cases, (d) caching and deduplication, (e) shorter prompts.
  4. How I'd verify each: Baseline arithmetic: 2M x 1,800 = 3.6B input tokens (about $32,400 per day at the illustrative price) plus 2M x 150 = 300M output tokens (about $13,500 per day). Test each lever against a human-labelled set of 300 cases: how much agreement and failure-class recall is lost?
  5. Root cause: Using the most expensive judge on every easy sample.
  6. Fix: Layered: code checks on 100% of traffic (free); a small, cheap judge on a 10% stratified sample; escalate low-confidence or disagreeing items and all flagged or negative-feedback responses to the strong judge; judge only responses that changed when re-evaluating; cache identical inputs; compress rubric tokens.
  7. Prevention: Track judge agreement vs a human sample monthly; track cost per scored response; alert when sample size per slice falls below what is needed for intervals.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Uniform sampling can miss rare slices, so stratify and oversample risky categories; I would not use the cheap judge for safety-critical decisions without validation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A rare failure at 0.05% rate. → Uniform 1% sampling would see about 10 per day at 2M; but target with detectors/flags rather than blind sampling.
  • Cheap judge kappa is 0.55 vs strong 0.72. → Use it only as a screen with a high-recall threshold.
  • Batch APIs? → For non-urgent grading, check provider batch pricing (verify).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's judge bill exceeded the generation bill; moving to a screen-then-escalate design cut cost 85% with no change in detected regressions on a labelled backlog.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random sampling or cheaper model without validation.
  • Hire: layered grading and sampling.
  • Strong hire: does the cost arithmetic, stratifies, validates each lever against humans, and monitors agreement over time.

questions.contextHtml: A booking agent passes its eval with 84% task success (single run per case, 250 cases). In production, the support team reports "it works sometimes": 31% of tickets in the last week concern tasks that fail on the first try and succeed on retry. A rerun of the eval with 5 samples per case shows per-case success varies: 150 cases always pass, 40 never pass, and 60 pass between 20% and 80% of the time. The team lead says the eval was fine since 84% is high.
questions.promptHtml: What did the eval miss, and how do you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Temperature is too high, set it to 0." It may help but does not explain what to measure, and a temperature of 0 does not remove all variance across tool calls and retrieval.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What temperature and sampling settings are used in production? Are tools or external systems non-deterministic? Where do failed runs diverge (planning, tool arguments, retrieval)? What is the cost of failure for the user?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a safe retry or confirmation step for known flaky flows and lower temperature for tool-calling steps while investigating.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) sampling variance in tool arguments and planning, (b) flaky downstream tools or API timeouts, (c) context differences between runs (retrieval ordering), (d) ambiguous tasks the agent resolves differently each time.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare traces of passing and failing runs for the 60 flaky cases; check tool error logs; fix seeds or stub tools to isolate agent variance from environment variance; cluster the divergent step.
  5. Root cause: A single-run metric reported expected success, not reliability. With 5 samples: 150 always pass (60%), 40 never (16%), and the 60 flaky cases (24%) contribute roughly half their runs; a quick estimate of pass^5 puts it well under 70% (the 60 flaky cases rarely pass all five).
  6. Fix: Report pass rate over k samples and pass^k, separate "always fail" (capability gap) from "sometimes fail" (reliability gap), and fix the flaky step with constrained decoding, clearer tool schemas, validation and retries.
  7. Prevention: Eval each case with multiple samples in the nightly tier; gate on pass^k for critical flows; trace-level assertions per step; monitor retry rates in production.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Multiple samples multiply eval cost, so use k=5 on a high-value subset and k=1 in fast CI; I would not hide flakiness with automatic retries without also measuring the first-try success.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Temperature 0 and still flaky. → Provider-side nondeterminism and tool variability remain; measure instead of assuming.
  • Retry fixes 31%. Done? → The user still waits twice; measure first-try success and latency.
  • How to separate environment flakiness? → Mock tools or record and replay tool responses.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scheduling agent's dashboard showed 90% success while support insisted otherwise; pass^3 turned out to be 55% and all of the variance came from one tool-argument step.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only lowers temperature.
  • Hire: recognizes single-run limits and proposes multiple samples.
  • Strong hire: introduces pass^k, splits capability from reliability failures, uses trace-level analysis and builds a gated reliability tier.
